items.question_text:
You used the gcloud container clusters command to create two Google Cloud Kubernetes (GKE) clusters: prod-cluster and dev-cluster.

• prod-cluster is a standard cluster.
• dev-cluster is an auto-pilot cluster.

When you run the kubectl get nodes command, you only see the nodes from prod-cluster. Which commands should you run to check the node status for dev-cluster?
items.solution_text: The gcloud container clusters get-credentials command is the standard method to update the kubeconfig file with the API server endpoint and authentication tokens for a specific GKE cluster. This action switches the active kubectl context, allowing subsequent commands like kubectl get nodes to target the specified dev-cluster instead of the default or previously selected cluster.

choices.text:
gcloud container clusters get-credentials dev-cluster
kubectl get nodes
gcloud container clusters update -generate-password dev-cluster kubectl get nodes

kubectl config set-context dev-cluster
kubectl cluster-info

kubectl config set-credentials dev-cluster
kubectl cluster-info

items.question_text:
You recently discovered that your developers are using many service account keys during their development process. While you work on a long term improvement, you need to quickly implement a process to enforce short-lived service account credentials in your company. You have the following requirements:

• All service accounts that require a key should be created in a centralized project called pj-sa.
• Service account keys should only be valid for one day.

You need a Google-recommended solution that minimizes cost. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Option C is correct because it uses Organization Policies to enforce the specific security requirements without incurring compute costs for rotation scripts.
The `constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountKeyCreation` constraint with an exception for `pj-sa` ensures keys are only created in the centralized project, while `constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyLifetimeLimitDays` enforces the 24-hour validity period.
This approach is Google-recommended and minimizes cost by relying on native IAM policies rather than running Cloud Run jobs or Kubernetes CronJobs for key rotation.

choices.text: Implement a Cloud Run job to rotate all service account keys periodically in pj-sa. Enforce an org policy to deny service account key creation with an exception to pj-sa.
Implement a Kubernetes CronJob to rotate all service account keys periodically. Disable attachment of service accounts to resources in all projects with an exception to pj-sa.
Enforce an org policy constraint allowing the lifetime of service account keys to be 24 hours. Enforce an org policy constraint denying service account key creation with an exception on pj-sa.
Enforce a DENY org policy constraint over the lifetime of service account keys for 24 hours. Disable attachment of service accounts to resources in all projects with an exception to pj-sa.

items.question_text: Your company is running a three-tier web application on virtual machines that use a MySQL database. You need to create an estimated total cost of cloud infrastructure to run this application on Google Cloud instances and Cloud SQL. What should you do?
items.solution_text: The Google Cloud Pricing Calculator is the designated tool for estimating infrastructure costs without incurring charges or deploying resources. Option D correctly describes using this calculator to model specific resources (Compute Engine instances and Cloud SQL) based on your current on-premises configurations for an accurate estimate. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because they involve manual spreadsheet work, non-existent templates, or unnecessary implementation of test infrastructure.

choices.text: Create a Google spreadsheet with multiple Google Cloud resource combinations. On a separate sheet, import the current Google Cloud prices and use these prices for the calculations within formulas.
Use the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator and select the Cloud Operations template to define your web application with as much detail as possible.

Implement a similar architecture on Google Cloud, and run a reasonable load test on a smaller scale. Check the billing information, and calculate the estimated costs based on the real load your system usually handles.

Use the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator to determine the cost of every Google Cloud resource you expect to use. Use similar size instances for the web server, and use your current on-premises machines as a comparison for Cloud SQL.

items.question_text: You have a Bigtable instance that consists of three nodes that store personally identifiable information (PII) data. You need to log all read or write operations, including any metadata or configuration reads of this database table, in your company’s Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. What should you do?
items.solution_text: To log all read and write operations on Bigtable data (including PII), you must enable Data Access audit logs (Data Read and Data Write), as they are disabled by default. Cloud Logging sinks provide the native mechanism to export these logs directly to a Pub/Sub topic, allowing your SIEM to subscribe and receive the data stream without custom code.

choices.text:
• Navigate to Cloud Monitoring in the Google Cloud console, and create a custom monitoring job for the Bigtable instance to track all changes.
• Create an alert by using webhook endpoints, with the SIEM endpoint as a receiver.

• Navigate to the Audit Logs page in the Google Cloud console, and enable Admin Write logs for the Bigtable instance.
• Create a Cloud Functions instance to export logs from Cloud Logging to your SIEM.

• Navigate to the Audit Logs page in the Google Cloud console, and enable Data Read, Data Write and Admin Read logs for the Bigtable instance.
• Create a Pub/Sub topic as a Cloud Logging sink destination, and add your SIEM as a subscriber to the topic.

• Install the Ops Agent on the Bigtable instance during configuration.
• Create a service account with read permissions for the Bigtable instance.
• Create a custom Dataflow job with this service account to export logs to the company’s SIEM system.

items.question_text: You want to set up a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Verifiable node identity and integrity are required for the cluster, and nodes cannot be accessed from the internet. You want to reduce the operational cost of managing your cluster, and you want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
items.solution_text: To minimize operational costs and follow Google-recommended practices, you should choose GKE Autopilot, which fully manages node provisioning and scaling. The requirement for nodes to be inaccessible from the internet mandates a private cluster configuration. Shielded GKE Nodes, which provide the required verifiable node identity and integrity, are enabled by default in Autopilot clusters.

choices.text: Deploy a private autopilot cluster.
Deploy a public autopilot cluster.
Deploy a standard public cluster and enable shielded nodes.
Deploy a standard private cluster and enable shielded nodes.
